problems.title: 3Sum

problems.title: Accounts Merge
problems.statement_markdown:

problems.title: Backend Product API: Run Dashboard
problems.statement_markdown:
## Task

**Coding. Purpose:** build a small useful product boundary around job state. Relevant to backend/API work for distributed databases and runtime products; the goal is a dashboard whose create/cancel actions and pagination behave predictably.

**60-minute core:** implement pure in-memory handlers, without an HTTP framework:

```text
create_run(tenant_id, request_id, payload) -> run
get_run(tenant_id, run_id) -> run | NOT_FOUND
cancel_run(tenant_id, run_id) -> run | NOT_FOUND
list_runs(tenant_id, limit, cursor?) -> page, next_cursor?
```

The caller's tenant identity is already authenticated; do not build login. Use immutable string payloads, unique monotonic internal run sequence numbers, and at most 1,000 retained runs. `create_run` reserves `(tenant_id, request_id)`: repeating it with the same payload returns the same run, while a different payload produces `CONFLICT`. This reservation remains valid for the exercise lifetime. New runs start `queued`. Cancellation transitions queued/running runs to `cancel_requested`; repeating it returns the current state. Succeeded, failed, and cancelled runs stay terminal. A private test helper may set worker states; implementing a worker is outside scope. Cross-tenant lookup/cancellation returns `NOT_FOUND`.

List newest first, with limits 1–100 and a cursor tied to the tenant. The first page captures a maximum sequence watermark. Later pages include only runs at or below that watermark and strictly below the last returned sequence. Cursor fields may be a validated tuple in this exercise; production cursor signing is discussion-only. No run deletion occurs. Validate wrong types and malformed cursors before mutation, and return copies or immutable records.

Local Python contract: implement `Dashboard`. Runs are dictionaries with `run_id`, `tenant_id`, `request_id`, `payload`, and `state`; return copies. `run_id` is the creation sequence, starting at 1. Return literal `CONFLICT` and `NOT_FOUND`. Tenant and request IDs are nonempty strings; payload may be an empty string. Invalid input raises `ValueError` (bool is not an integer). Run IDs are positive integers. Exhausting the 1,000-run limit raises `RuntimeError`, but existing request retries still deduplicate or conflict. `list_runs` returns `(runs, next_cursor)`; `None` means no more pages. A cursor is exactly `(tenant_id, watermark, last)`, with positive integer bounds and `last <= watermark`, and must match the caller tenant. Omitted cursor or `None` starts a new page sequence. The watermark is the tenant's maximum sequence at the first page. `_set_state(run_id, state)` is a test-only hook for simulating worker states, not a public handler. Extensions are discussion-only.

## Example

tenant A creates sequence 1 and 2; tenant B creates sequence 3. A requests limit 1 and sees sequence 2 plus cursor `(watermark=2,last=2)`. A then creates sequence 4. Its next page returns sequence 1, never B's sequence 3 or newly inserted sequence 4. Repeating sequence 2's create request returns the same ID. Changing its payload returns conflict.

**Acceptance cases:** duplicate request/same payload; duplicate/different payload; cross-tenant access; empty page; exact final page; inserted run between pages; terminal cancellation; repeated cancellation; invalid limit/cursor. State that a cancellation request is an observable intent, not proof an external job stopped.

**Extension:** move handlers into two API replicas sharing a database. Identify required uniqueness constraints and atomic state updates. Explain why a process-local dictionary or mutex no longer protects deduplication or cancellation races.

problems.title: Bounded Asynchronous Job Runner
problems.statement_markdown:
## Task

**Coding. Purpose:** demonstrate backpressure, task lifetime, failure isolation, and shutdown. Relevant to runtime/tool execution and the scheduler theme in Fireworks notes; this is an original drill.

**60-minute core:** implement a Python `asyncio` runner:

```text
Runner(worker_count, queue_capacity)
await start()
submit(job_id, async_callable) -> accepted | queue_full
status(job_id) -> state | NOT_FOUND
cancel(job_id) -> state | NOT_FOUND
await close() -> outcomes_by_id
```

`submit` is synchronous and must not create an unbounded population of waiting tasks. Allow 1–16 workers and 1–100 queued jobs. A job is a zero-argument async callable; invoke it to create its coroutine only when a worker is ready. IDs are unique for the runner lifetime, including rejected retry policy: queue-full submissions do not reserve their ID, accepted submissions do. Reject duplicate accepted IDs. Preserve FIFO dequeue order, but completion order can differ. Job exceptions become failure outcomes and do not kill a worker. `close` stops admission, drains accepted work, stops workers, and returns each accepted ID exactly once. Repeated `close` returns the same outcomes. Calls happen on one event loop; job code eventually returns or raises. Bound accepted jobs to 1,000 for the exercise so outcome retention is explicit.

**Status and cancellation:** expose `queued`, `running`, `succeeded`, `failed`, and `cancelled`. Cancelling a queued job marks it cancelled and prevents execution; its queue slot may remain occupied until dequeued. Cancelling a running job requests cooperative task cancellation, with state remaining running until execution acknowledges it. If completion wins the race, preserve the completed outcome. Terminal cancellation is a no-op. For this core, jobs yield to the event loop and do not suppress cancellation. Cancelled accepted jobs still appear exactly once in close outcomes.

Local Python contract: implement `Runner`. Return literal strings for admission, states, and `NOT_FOUND`; `close()` returns `{job_id: terminal_state}` (job values and exception objects are outside the result contract). IDs must be nonempty strings. Invalid arguments (including bool instead of int), duplicate accepted IDs, or a non-callable job raise `ValueError`. Capacity is 1,000 accepted jobs over the lifetime; exceeding it raises `RuntimeError`. Admission before start or after closing raises `RuntimeError`. Call `start()` once before other lifecycle operations; repeated start raises `RuntimeError`. Empty close means a started runner with no jobs. All public methods run on the same event loop. Extensions are discussion-only.

## Example

with one worker, hold A inside an event-controlled job. Queue B and C with queue capacity 2. D returns `queue_full`. Release A; B raises `ValueError`; C succeeds. Closing returns one success for A, one failure for B, and one success for C, with no D outcome. The worker survives B.

**Acceptance cases:** queue at capacity; duplicate ID; submission after close; empty close; failing job; queued and running cancellation; completion/cancellation race; FIFO start order; all accepted jobs accounted for. Use events to hold running work; a race between worker scheduling and submission should not make the expected queue state ambiguous.

**Extension:** support `close(timeout)` and relax the assumption that jobs cooperate with cancellation. Specify whether queued jobs become cancelled outcomes and what happens if job code suppresses cancellation. Do not promise a hard deadline for arbitrary Python code in one process.

problems.title: Buy the Cheapest Available Items
problems.statement_markdown:
## Task

**Coding. Purpose:** turn an underspecified marketplace story into a deterministic data model and an incremental implementation. This is a reconstruction of the reported prompt, not an exact transcription or a financial exchange order book.

**60-minute core:** implement an in-memory inventory with:

```text
add(listing_id, item, seller, unit_price_cents, quantity)
buy(item, requested_quantity, max_unit_price_cents) -> fills, unfilled_quantity
cancel(listing_id) -> bool
```

Listing IDs are unique for the process lifetime. Item/seller/ID are nonempty strings; prices are nonnegative integers; quantities are positive integers. Reject invalid input before mutation. Each listing has a fixed price and a monotonic insertion sequence. A buy consumes available listings at or below the price ceiling, cheapest first, then oldest first. Partial fills are allowed. A fill is `(listing_id, seller, quantity, unit_price_cents)`; return fills in execution order. Unknown cancellation returns false; exhausted listings cannot fill again. Assume sequential calls, one currency, and at most 10,000 listings. A straightforward correct scan/sort is acceptable; state its cost before choosing a more complex index.

Local practice contract: Implement `Inventory`. Invalid arguments and duplicate IDs raise `ValueError`; bool does not count as an integer. All IDs remain reserved after acceptance, even after cancellation or exhaustion. Cancelling an exhausted listing returns false. Exceeding the 10,000 lifetime listing limit raises `RuntimeError`. Extensions are optional follow-ups.

## Example

**Worked example:** add L1 apple/alice at 500 cents with quantity 2; L2 apple/bob at 400 with quantity 1; L3 apple/carol at 500 with quantity 3. `buy(apple, 4, 500)` yields `[(L2,bob,1,400), (L1,alice,2,500), (L3,carol,1,500)]`, unfilled 0. L3 retains 2. A later `buy(apple,3,450)` returns no fills and unfilled 3. Cancelling L3 returns true.

**Acceptance cases:** missing item; no affordable listing; exact exhaustion; partial fill; equal prices; cancellation followed by a buy; duplicate ID; invalid quantity; no state change after invalid input. Explain whether integer overflow matters in the chosen language before adding total-cost arithmetic.

**Extension:** add `all_or_none=True`. If affordable stock is insufficient, consume nothing. Discuss a concurrent caller arriving between availability checking and consumption; implementing concurrency is outside the base exercise.

problems.title: Deadlock-Aware Lock Manager
problems.statement_markdown:
## Task

**Coding. Purpose:** reason about ownership, waiting, and the atomic decision to admit a blocking acquisition. This revisits an actual past prompt without treating the old attempt as a solution.

**60-minute core:** implement `safe_lock(lock)` and `safe_unlock(lock)` in Python for a single manager and a bounded set of ordinary, non-reentrant thread locks. Every acquisition and release goes through this manager. A thread may own several locks but has at most one pending acquisition. `safe_lock` returns only after acquisition; it raises `DeadlockedAttempt` if the requested wait would close a cycle. Reacquiring a lock the caller owns raises that same exception. Releasing a lock owned by another thread is an error. Fairness, timeouts, process death, and mixing managers are outside the core. Use explicit synchronization rather than relying on the GIL.

The manager must actually provide mutual exclusion, not merely update a dictionary. Choose and explain one ownership-transfer protocol. It may coordinate logical ownership using a condition variable, provided the supplied locks are acquired and released consistently and no caller can bypass the manager. Do not hold the manager's metadata mutex while waiting for a lock owner to release.

Local practice contract: Implement `LockManager`. The supplied `DeadlockedAttempt` name aliases `RuntimeError`; invalid unlock raises `ValueError`. Use ordinary `threading.Lock` instances. Extensions are optional follow-ups.

## Example

**Worked scenario:** T1 holds A; T2 holds B. T1 asks for B and blocks. T2 asks for A and gets `DeadlockedAttempt`; T2 still owns B. T2's caller releases B in cleanup, allowing T1 to acquire B. The rejection does not silently release locks or roll back the caller's work.

**Acceptance cases:** uncontended acquisition; several locks owned by one thread; contention without a cycle; two-thread and three-thread cycles; self-acquisition; invalid unlock; clean metadata after release. Use barriers/events to create ordering instead of assuming a sleep proves correctness. Test joins need bounded timeouts so a broken implementation does not hang the rehearsal.

**Extension:** add an acquisition timeout. Describe precisely how timing out removes a wait edge and how a simultaneous release is resolved. Implement only after the cycle-checking core works.

problems.title: Debug a Python Service with pdb
problems.statement_markdown:
## Task

**Debugging. Purpose:** build a causal explanation from a failing user path, then make the smallest verified repair. This is an original fixture, not a disclosed employer task. The snippet is intentionally defective; copy it into a temporary `service_debug.py`, never a production service.

**60-minute core:** investigate why a request appears to disappear after an upstream failure. The intended API accepts requests in FIFO order. Every request must produce exactly one immutable result containing its own ID. A failed upstream call produces a failure result; later requests still complete. The exercise has no retry, cancellation, concurrency, or external network access.

```python
from collections import deque


def fake_upstream(request):
    if request["id"] == "B":
        raise ValueError("upstream rejected B")
    return request["value"] * 2


def drain(pending, results):
    response = {}
    while pending:
        request = pending.popleft()
        try:
            response["id"] = request["id"]
            response["value"] = fake_upstream(request)
            response["ok"] = True
            results.append(response)
        except ValueError as error:
            response["ok"] = False
            response["error"] = str(error)
            if pending:
                pending.popleft()
    return results


if __name__ == "__main__":
    requests = deque([
        {"id": "A", "value": 2},
        {"id": "B", "value": 3},
        {"id": "C", "value": 4},
    ])
    print(drain(requests, []))
```

Local practice contract: The intentionally defective fixture is already in `python/problems/medium/service_debug.py`. Run it directly, then use `python3 -m pdb python/problems/medium/service_debug.py`. Repair `drain`, preserving the fake upstream behavior. The judge compares fresh result dictionaries; records must never be mutated by later processing. Tests should fail before you repair the fixture. Extensions are optional follow-ups.

## Example

**Expected result contract:** A yields `{id: A, ok: true, value: 4}`; B yields `{id: B, ok: false, error: "upstream rejected B"}`; C yields `{id: C, ok: true, value: 8}`. Failure records have no value field; success records have no error field. The exact printed Python representation may use single quotes.

**Investigation:** first run `python service_debug.py` and record the actual output. Then use `python -m pdb service_debug.py`; demonstrate `break`/`b`, `continue`/`c`, `next`/`n`, `step`/`s`, `where`/`w`, `p`, and `pp` where useful. Stop around dequeue, append, and the exception branch. Inspect queue contents, `id(response)`, and previously appended results before changing code. Name each independent defect and connect it to the symptom. Avoid evaluating destructive expressions such as `p pending.popleft()` in the debugger.

**Acceptance cases:** the three-request scenario; two successes; failure first; failure last; empty input. Deliver a short causal account, a focused patch, and a regression check. No full framework or logging rewrite is needed.

**Extension:** introduce a retryable exception with at most two total attempts per request. Preserve original FIFO processing and final-result order; terminal failures still produce one result. Explain why retrying an upstream side effect may require an idempotency contract.

problems.title: Durable Agent Execution with External Tools
problems.statement_markdown:
## Task

**System design. Purpose:** connect runtime experience to Normal's agent-systems domain without claiming prior production agent ownership.

**60-minute core:** design a single-region service that runs a fixed sequence of up to 20 steps per run. A step either calls a model, calls an external tool, or waits for human approval. Invented sizing assumptions: 10 new runs/second, up to 10,000 active runs, 24-hour maximum run duration, 1 MiB maximum persisted run state, 30-day history retention. A transactional database and at-least-once queue are available. Model and tool results can vary between attempts. Model calls may retry; a payment-like tool offers an idempotency key and a lookup API. Do not implement a planner, train a model, or invent consensus.

Define `start(client_request_id, workflow_version, input)`, `status(run_id)`, `approve(run_id, step_id, decision_id)`, and `cancel(run_id)`. Draw persisted run/step/attempt records and the transition that grants execution ownership. Explain which data must survive worker loss and how a new worker resumes. Cancellation stops future work; specify what it can promise about an already issued external call. Include a trace from user request to final outcome.

Local practice contract: This is a system-design rehearsal, not a coding task. Use the prompt to produce a request trace, failure trace, persisted data model, sizing estimate, and explicit limitations. There is no executable adapter or automated pass/fail grade. Extensions are optional follow-ups.

## Example

**Failure scenario:** worker W1 sends tool operation K; the provider completes it; W1 dies before storing the result. W2 receives the run again. It must recover K's result or reuse K safely, not issue a new operation identity. A duplicate approval arrives after step completion and must not advance the workflow twice.

**Extension:** the tool provides neither idempotency nor lookup. Decide how the product exposes an uncertain outcome and when human reconciliation is necessary. “Exactly once” is not an acceptable unexplained answer.

problems.title: GPU Inference Routing and Capacity
problems.statement_markdown:
## Task

**System design. Purpose:** use serving, lifecycle, and capacity experience to reason about Fireworks-relevant tradeoffs without drifting into unsupported kernel expertise.

**60-minute core:** design one-region routing for two model revisions and streaming inference. All numbers are exercise assumptions. Each replica uses two GPUs, takes 90 seconds to become ready, and sustains 100 requests/second for a measured reference workload. Normal load is 600 requests/second; one model can burst to 1,200 for five minutes. Total limit is 32 GPUs. Target headroom is 20%; accepted requests target time-to-first-token below one second. A replica is not routable until weights are loaded and a representative readiness probe passes. Define admission, bounded queues, routing metadata, streaming ownership, draining, and scaling signals. State when the SLO cannot be met rather than promising it under arbitrary bursts.

Local practice contract: This is a system-design rehearsal, not a coding task. Produce a request trace, failure trace, capacity estimate, and explicit limitations. There is no executable adapter or automated pass/fail grade. Extensions are optional follow-ups.

## Example

**Worked sizing:** reference-workload steady demand at 80% of measured replica capacity requires `ceil(600 / 80) = 8` replicas, or 16 GPUs. Burst demand requires 15 replicas, or 30 GPUs. Splitting those GPUs across models and revisions can leave the hot model short; a GPU count is not instantly usable model-specific capacity. At a sudden burst, waiting 90 seconds for capacity cannot meet a one-second TTFT target, so choose prewarmed capacity, overflow, or explicit rejection.

**Failure scenario:** a gateway has an endpoint cached as ready while the replica begins draining. The replica must stop admitting new requests without abruptly terminating healthy streams; the gateway needs a bounded, safe response to a rejected new stream. After bytes have been sent to the client, transparently replaying the entire generation is not generally safe.

**Extension:** prompts become 10× longer while request rate stays constant. Explain why requests/second alone becomes misleading, and how token rates, KV-cache pressure, queue time, and measured workload classes change sizing. No CUDA implementation is required.

problems.title: LRU Cache
problems.statement_markdown:
## Task

Design a fixed-capacity cache with `get(key)` and `put(key, value)` operations. Both operations mark an existing key as recently used. Inserting a new key into a full cache evicts the least recently used key, and `get` returns `-1` for a missing key.

## Example

With capacity `2`, operations `put(1, 1)`, `put(2, 2)`, `get(1)`, `put(3, 3)`, and `get(2)` return `1` from the first read and `-1` from the second because key `2` was evicted.

problems.title: Optimistic Transaction Store
problems.statement_markdown:
## Task

**Coding. Purpose:** explain the version and atomicity machinery behind safe optimistic updates. Adapted from the local distributed database preparation drill.

**60-minute core:** implement:

```text
store.begin() -> transaction
transaction.read(key) -> integer | MISSING
transaction.write(key, integer)
transaction.commit() -> commit_version | CONFLICT
transaction.abort()
```

Use nonempty string keys and immutable integer values. Calls on a transaction are sequential; store commits may race. Reads return staged writes first. On first access to a key, including a blind write, record its current version. Repeated reads of a previously read key return its cached value. A missing key has an observable version. Commit validates every observed key and applies all staged writes atomically under one store synchronization boundary. Any mismatch produces `CONFLICT`, closes the transaction, and applies nothing. Successful write commits assign one shared increasing version to their writes. Read-only commits validate and return the current global version without advancing it. All operations on a closed transaction fail. Abort closes an active transaction; repeated abort fails. No deletes, ranges, external side effects, persistence, or historical snapshots.

This is a point-access OCC exercise. Transactions do not begin with a complete historical snapshot; a transaction that sees incompatible moments must fail validation. Do not describe uncommitted reads as a full database snapshot guarantee.

Local practice contract: Implement `Store` and `Transaction`. Use the supplied string constants `MISSING` and `CONFLICT`. The initial global version is 0. Invalid keys or values raise `ValueError`; bool is not an integer. Closed-transaction operations raise `RuntimeError`. Extensions are optional follow-ups.

## Example

**Worked scenario:** initial `x=10@v1`. A and B both read x=10. A writes x=11 and commits v2. B stages `y=20` and commits: conflict because its observed x version is stale; y remains missing. Separately, C and D both first access missing z and stage writes. After C commits, D must conflict even though z was absent when D observed it.

**Acceptance cases:** read own write; stale read; blind-write race; competing missing-key insertions; multi-key atomic failure; read-only commit; closed state rejection. Use an actual absence marker rather than a possible user value.

**Extension:** add deletion without allowing version history to reset to “never existed.” Explain a delete/reinsert sequence and tombstone/version retention. Range-query phantoms are a discussion-only follow-up.

problems.title: Pacific Atlantic Water Flow
problems.statement_markdown:

Given a height grid, return coordinates from which water can reach both the top-or-left boundary and the bottom-or-right boundary by moving to an equal or lower neighbor. Coordinate ordering is unrestricted.

## Example

For heights `[[1,2,2,3,5], [3,2,3,4,4], [2,4,5,3,1], [6,7,1,4,5], [5,1,1,2,4]]`, the result is `[[0,4], [1,3], [1,4], [2,2], [3,0], [3,1], [4,0]]`; coordinate ordering is unrestricted.

problems.title: Reactive Subscription Invalidation Index
problems.statement_markdown:
## Task

**Coding. Purpose:** maintain consistent forward/reverse indexes and define honest overload behavior. Adapted from the local distributed database subscription drill; public product architecture motivates it, not an exact question report.

**60-minute core:** implement:

```text
subscribe(subscription_id, dependency_keys)
unsubscribe(subscription_id) -> bool
dependencies(subscription_id) -> set | NOT_FOUND
invalidate(changed_keys, max_results) -> sorted_subscription_ids | OVERLOAD
```

IDs and keys are nonempty strings. Maximum 1,000 subscriptions, 32 distinct dependencies per subscription, and 128 distinct changed keys per invalidation. Validate complete input before mutation. Re-subscribing replaces the dependency set; duplicates within inputs collapse. An empty dependency set is a valid subscription. Unknown unsubscribe returns false. `max_results` is an integer from 0 through 1,000. Return each affected subscription once in lexicographic order. An overflow returns only `OVERLOAD`, with no partial successful result. Invalidation is read-only and does not remove subscriptions. All calls are sequential; return copies to prevent caller mutation of internal state.

Local practice contract: Implement `SubscriptionIndex`. Return literal strings `NOT_FOUND` and `OVERLOAD`. Invalid inputs or resource limits raise `ValueError`; bool is not an integer. Key inputs are finite iterables of strings, not a bare string. Reject invalid replacement before changing the existing subscription. Extensions are optional follow-ups.

## Example

**Worked example:** subscribe s2 to `{a,b}` and s1 to `{b,c}`. Invalidating `{b,c}` with limit 2 returns `[s1,s2]`; limit 1 returns `OVERLOAD`. Replace s2 with `{d}`; invalidating `{a,b}` returns `[s1]`, and the reverse entry for a must disappear. Unsubscribe s1; invalidating b returns `[]`.

**Acceptance cases:** replacement; shared keys; duplicate changed keys; empty dependencies; exact limit; one beyond limit; zero limit with/without matches; invalid replacement preserving the original; caller mutation of returned dependencies. State memory complexity in total dependency edges.

**Extension:** one key affects a million subscriptions. Design a resumable invalidation work item with a clear coverage guarantee while subscriptions change. Implementing distributed fanout is outside the 60-minute core.

problems.title: Remove Nth Node From End of List
problems.statement_markdown:

Given a linked-list head and one-based position `n` from the tail, remove that node and return the resulting head.

## Example

List `[1, 2, 3, 4, 5]` with `n = 2` returns `[1, 2, 3, 5]`.

problems.statement_markdown:

Given a linked-list head, mutate it in place by alternating nodes from the front and back. Return no value.

List `[1, 2, 3, 4]` is mutated to `[1, 4, 2, 3]`.

problems.title: Reverse Bits
problems.statement_markdown:
## Task

Interpret the input as a 32-bit bit pattern, reverse its bit positions, and return the resulting 32-bit pattern. The Rust adapter represents both patterns as `i32`; signedness does not change the bits being reversed.

## Example

Input pattern `43261596` returns pattern `964176192`.

problems.title: Reverse Linked List
problems.statement_markdown:
## Task

Given a linked-list head, reverse its links and return the new head.

## Example

List `[1, 2, 3, 4, 5]` returns `[5, 4, 3, 2, 1]`.

problems.title: Rotate Image
problems.statement_markdown:
## Task

Given a square matrix, rotate it 90 degrees clockwise in place and return no value.

## Example

Matrix `[[1,2,3], [4,5,6], [7,8,9]]` becomes `[[7,4,1], [8,5,2], [9,6,3]]`.

problems.title: Reproducible Builds and Safe Deployment Rollout
problems.statement_markdown:
## Task

**System design. Purpose:** rehearse a second architecture lane involving developer tooling, asynchronous builds, immutable artifacts, and serving state. This is an original platform drill, not a claim that Fireworks uses this architecture.

**60-minute core:** design `deploy(app_id, source_digest, config, request_id)` and `get_deployment(deployment_id)` for customer Python inference services. Assume 1,000 deployments/day, builds lasting up to 10 minutes, a maximum of 20 concurrent builds, an artifact registry, a transactional database, and a Kubernetes-like scheduler. Customers expect build logs, a terminal outcome, and the previous healthy version to keep serving if the new build fails. Code can be untrusted. Define build identity, queuing, isolation boundary, artifact identity, deployment state, readiness, traffic switch, and rollback. No multi-region rollout or custom package manager is required.

Local practice contract: This is a system-design rehearsal, not a coding task. Produce a deploy-to-traffic trace, failure trace, data model, sizing estimate, and explicit limitations. There is no executable adapter or automated pass/fail grade. Extensions are optional follow-ups.

## Example

**Worked scenario:** deploy D2 while D1 serves traffic. D2 builds artifact digest H2 but its startup probe fails. D1 continues serving; D2 reaches a failed state with its build/runtime diagnostic. A retry using the same request ID returns the original deployment rather than starting another build. A genuinely new request may retry with a new deployment ID. Logs must not expose build secrets.

**Extension:** D3 is requested before D2 finishes, and D2 becomes healthy last. Specify whether last-requested-wins or serialized promotion applies. Show the version/check that prevents D2 from replacing the newer desired revision. Discuss cancellation of obsolete builds without losing their history.

problems.title: Same Tree
problems.statement_markdown:
## Task

Given two binary-tree roots, return whether both trees have the same shape and equal values at corresponding nodes.

## Example

Trees `[1, 2, 3]` and `[1, 2, 3]` return `true`.

problems.title: Search in Rotated Sorted Array
problems.statement_markdown:
## Task

Given a rotated sorted integer list and a target, return the index where the target occurs. If the target is absent, return the sentinel `-1`.

## Example

List `[4, 5, 6, 7, 0, 1, 2]` with target `0` returns `4`.

problems.title: Serialize and Deserialize Binary Tree
problems.statement_markdown:
## Task

Create or initialize a tree codec that can serialize a tree as a string and deserialize that string to reconstruct the tree. Only round-trip tree structure and values are prescribed; any encoding format is valid.

## Example

Create a codec, serialize tree `[1, 2, 3, null, null, 4, 5]`, then deserialize the encoded value; the result is an equivalent tree.

problems.title: Set Matrix Zeroes
problems.statement_markdown:
## Task

Given a matrix, mutate it in place so every row and column containing an input zero becomes all zeroes. Return no value.

## Example

Matrix `[[1,1,1], [1,0,1], [1,1,1]]` becomes `[[1,0,1], [0,0,0], [1,0,1]]`.

problems.title: Sliding Window Maximum
problems.statement_markdown:
## Task

Given an integer list and a positive window size `k`, return the maximum value in each contiguous window as the window moves from left to right.

## Example

Input `[1, 3, -1, -3, 5, 3, 6, 7]` with `k = 3` returns `[3, 3, 5, 5, 6, 7]`.

problems.title: Spiral Matrix
problems.statement_markdown:
## Task

Given a matrix, return its values in clockwise spiral order starting at the top-left corner.

## Example

Input `[[1,2,3], [4,5,6], [7,8,9]]` returns `[1,2,3,6,9,8,7,4,5]`.

problems.title: Subarray Sum Equals K
problems.statement_markdown:
## Task

Given an integer list and target `k`, return the number of contiguous nonempty subarrays whose values sum to `k`.

## Example

List `[1, 1, 1]` with `k = 2` returns `2`.

problems.title: Subsets
problems.statement_markdown:
## Task

Given a list of distinct integers, return every subset, including the empty set and the full input. Values within each subset and subsets within the result may appear in any order.

## Example

Input `[1, 2]` returns `[]`, `[1]`, `[2]`, and `[1, 2]`.

problems.title: Subtree of Another Tree
problems.statement_markdown:
## Task

Given roots of two binary trees, return whether the second tree occurs in the first with identical shape and values.

## Example

Tree `[3, 4, 5, 1, 2]` and candidate `[4, 1, 2]` return `true`.

problems.title: Sum of Two Integers
problems.statement_markdown:
## Task

Given two integers, return their sum.

## Example

Inputs `2` and `3` return `5`.

problems.title: Time Based Key-Value Store
problems.statement_markdown:
## Task

Design a string key-value store whose `set(key, value, timestamp)` calls arrive with strictly increasing timestamps for each key. `get(key, timestamp)` returns the value recorded at the greatest timestamp not exceeding the requested time, or an empty string when no such value exists.

## Example

After `set("foo", "bar", 1)`, reads of `"foo"` at times `1` and `3` both return `"bar"`. After `set("foo", "bar2", 4)`, a read at time `5` returns `"bar2"`.

problems.title: Top K Frequent Elements
problems.statement_markdown:
## Task

Given an integer list and `k`, return `k` values with the greatest occurrence counts in any order. If several values tie at the frequency boundary for the final positions, any selection among those tied values is valid.

## Example

List `[1, 1, 1, 2, 2, 3]` with `k = 2` returns values `1` and `2`.

problems.title: Two Sum
problems.statement_markdown:
## Task

Given an integer list and target, return two distinct valid indices whose values sum to the target. Index ordering is unrestricted.

## Example

List `[2, 7, 11, 15]` with target `9` returns indices `0` and `1`.

problems.title: Two Sum II - Input Array Is Sorted
problems.statement_markdown:
## Task

Given a nondecreasing integer list and a target with exactly one valid pair, return the distinct pair's one-based indices in increasing order.

## Example

List `[2, 7, 11, 15]` with target `9` returns `[1, 2]`.

problems.title: Unique Paths
problems.statement_markdown:
## Task

Given grid dimensions `rows` and `columns`, return the number of paths from the top-left to bottom-right when each move goes right or down.

## Example

Dimensions `3` by `7` return `28`.

problems.title: Valid Anagram
problems.statement_markdown:
## Task

Given two strings, return whether they contain exactly the same characters with the same counts.

## Example

Inputs `"anagram"` and `"nagaram"` return `true`.

problems.title: Valid Palindrome
problems.statement_markdown:
## Task

Given a string, ignore non-alphanumeric characters and letter case, then return whether the remaining characters form a palindrome.

## Example

Input `"A man, a plan, a canal: Panama"` returns `true`.

problems.title: Valid Parentheses
problems.statement_markdown:
## Task

Given a string of bracket characters, return whether every opening bracket is closed by the matching type in properly nested order.

## Example

Input `"()[]{}"` returns `true`.

problems.title: Validate Binary Search Tree
problems.statement_markdown:
## Task

Given a binary-tree root, return whether every node obeys strict binary-search-tree ordering throughout its subtrees.

## Example

Tree `[2, 1, 3]` returns `true`.

problems.title: Word Break
problems.statement_markdown:
## Task

Given a string and dictionary of words, return whether the string can be split into a sequence of dictionary entries.

## Example

String `"leetcode"` with dictionary `["leet", "code"]` returns `true`.

problems.title: Word Search
problems.statement_markdown:
## Task

Given a character grid and a word, return whether the word can be formed by vertically or horizontally adjacent cells. Each grid cell may be used at most once in one word.

## Example

Grid `[["A", "B", "C", "E"], ["S", "F", "C", "S"], ["A", "D", "E", "E"]]` returns `true` for `"ABCCED"`.

problems.title: Word Search II
problems.statement_markdown:
## Task

Given a character grid and candidate words, return every candidate that can be formed by vertically or horizontally adjacent cells without reusing a cell within one word. Result ordering is unrestricted.

## Example

Grid `[["o", "a", "a", "n"], ["e", "t", "a", "e"], ["i", "h", "k", "r"], ["i", "f", "l", "v"]]` with words `["oath", "pea", "eat", "rain"]` returns `["eat", "oath"]` in either order.
